title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 146
paragraphs: So spoke Charilaos, and Maiandrios accepted what he said—not, I think, because he had reached such a pitch of folly as to suppose his own power would overcome the king's, but because he begrudged Syloson that he should receive the state without trouble and with no harm done to it. He therefore wished to provoke the Persians to anger and make the Samian power as feeble as possible before surrendering it, being well assured that the Persians, when they had suffered harm, were likely to be as bitter against the Samians as against those who had wronged them. He also knew he had a safe way of escape from the island whenever he wished, for he had had a secret passage made underground from the fortress to the sea. Maiandrios himself then sailed out from Samos; but Charilaos armed all the mercenaries, threw the gates wide, and sent them out upon the Persians, who were expecting no such thing but supposed everything had been arranged. The mercenaries, falling upon them, began to kill the Persians who had chairs carried out for them and were of most account. While these were thus engaged, the rest of the Persian force came to the rescue, and the mercenaries were hard pressed and forced to retire into the fortress.
